tieu_de: Eclipses in the birth chart: what they actually do, and what they don't
mo: Reading an eclipse by natal contact

Eclipses get more dramatic press than anything else in astrology. "Everything changes." "Fated events." "Don't sign anything." Some of that is earned; most of it is volume. An eclipse is a New or Full Moon with the lunar nodes involved, and its effect on you depends almost entirely on one question: does it touch your chart?

This guide covers what an eclipse is astronomically, the difference between solar and lunar eclipses, the eclipse seasons and the 18-month theme, how to read an eclipse by house and by natal contact, the Saros connection, and the most useful part: how to tell whether a given eclipse is yours at all.

doan: The Moon's orbit is tilted about five degrees to the Sun's path. The two points where they cross are the lunar nodes. Most New and Full Moons happen with the Moon above or below the Sun's line, so nothing lines up. But when a New or Full Moon falls within about 18 degrees of a node, the Sun, Moon, and Earth align closely enough to cast a shadow: an eclipse.

Astrologically, an eclipse is a lunation (a New or Full Moon) that's also tied to the nodes, which carry the meaning of direction, fate, and adjustment. So it's a beginning or culmination with a sense of consequence attached.
Planet Moon Rules Cancer Emotions, intuition, nurturing
Planet Sun Rules Leo Ego, will, vitality

Solar eclipse = New Moon near a node. The Moon blocks the Sun. Theme: a beginning, a new chapter, something entering. Often felt as an external event that opens a door, or as a sudden absence that makes room.
Lunar eclipse = Full Moon near a node. The Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. Theme: a culmination, an ending, a revelation. Something comes to light or comes to an end, often emotionally charged.
The pairing usually goes: a solar eclipse starts a story, and the lunar eclipse two weeks before or after it shows what has to be released for the story to proceed.

Eclipses come in seasons: twice a year, about 5.5 months apart, with two (occasionally three) eclipses in each season. The nodes move backwards through the zodiac, so each season's eclipses fall in a sign pair (say, Aries-Libra), and that pair stays active for about 18 months before the nodes shift to the previous pair (Pisces-Virgo).

That 18-month window is the eclipse theme. If the eclipses are in your 4th and 10th houses for a year and a half, home and career are being restructured over that whole period, with each eclipse marking a step. Knowing the current sign pair, and which houses it hits in your chart, is the single most useful fact about eclipses.
Find the house the eclipse degree falls in. The reading is the same as a New or Full Moon in that house, with the volume up and the timeline extended to months.
1st/7th axis: self and partnership. Identity shifts; relationships begin or end.
2nd/8th: money, values, shared resources. Financial restructuring; inheritance, debt, intimacy.
3rd/9th: communication and belief. Study, travel, siblings, publishing, a change of mind.
4th/10th: home and career. Moves, family changes, career pivots, public exposure.
5th/11th: creativity, children, friends, goals. Romance, pregnancy, group involvement, a long-term aim redirected.
6th/12th: work, health, the hidden. Job changes, health issues, endings behind the scenes.
The eclipse activates the house it's in most directly, and the opposite house through the axis.

muc.ten: Reading an eclipse by natal contact
doan: The house gives the area. A natal contact makes it personal. An eclipse within about 3 degrees of a natal planet or angle is an eclipse that will be felt.
On the Sun: identity, direction, or the father; a major personal turning point.
On the Moon: emotional life, home, the mother; a change in what you need.
On the Ascendant: you change, visibly; new start, new look, new health.
On the Midheaven: career or public standing shifts, often suddenly.
On Venus: love and money; a relationship begins or ends, or a financial reset.
On Mars: action, anger, or the body; something forces a move.
On Saturn: structure tested; a responsibility ends or a wall comes down.
On Jupiter: expansion, often welcome; a big opportunity or a big overreach.
On the outer planets: slower, generational; usually felt only if the planet is angular.
An eclipse with no natal contact within about 3 degrees is a background event. It sets a theme for the house but rarely produces a specific event.
Eclipse effects don't happen on the day. The common pattern:
Weeks before: the theme starts to surface, often as a feeling that something is coming.
At the eclipse, plus or minus a few days: an event, a decision, a revelation, or nothing obvious.
Weeks and months after: the real unfolding, especially when a transiting planet (often Mars) crosses the eclipse degree and triggers it.

Some astrologers hold that an eclipse's effects last until the next eclipse in the same house, six months later. In practice the strongest window is a couple of weeks either side, with aftershocks at later transits to the degree.

Every 9.3 years, eclipses fall on your natal nodal axis: at about 9, 18.5, 28, 37, 46, 56. These are the eclipses that matter most, because they hit the part of the chart that's already about direction. They coincide with the nodal return and the nodal reversal, and they tend to mark the turning points people describe when they tell the story of their lives.
If you're in one of those years, this guide's "is it yours?" question answers itself.
Two older ideas that still get used:

The prenatal eclipse is the last eclipse before your birth. Its degree is a sensitive point in your chart for life; transits to it and later eclipses near it are significant. Some astrologers read it as a theme you were born into.

Saros families: eclipses repeat in cycles of about 18 years and 11 days, and each cycle belongs to a numbered family with its own character. An eclipse from the same family as your prenatal eclipse, or as an eclipse that marked a past event, is worth watching. This is deep-end material, and worth exploring once the basics above feel familiar.
The question that saves you from eclipse anxiety. Run through it for each eclipse:
Which of my houses does it fall in? (Everyone gets this. It's the theme.)
Is it within 3 degrees of a natal planet or angle? (If no, it's background.)
Is it within 3 degrees of my natal nodes? (If yes, it's a life marker.)
Is it on my prenatal eclipse degree? (If yes, extra weight.)

Most eclipses are "no" to 2, 3, and 4 for most people. Those eclipses set a mood in a house and nothing more. The ones that are "yes" are the ones to prepare for, and they come along maybe once or twice a year, not every season.
